title: 73rd and 74th Amendments

cards.b:
India's Constitution was first written with two levels of government: the Union and the states. Villages and towns were left to state law, with only a weak Directive Principle (Article 40) asking the State to organise village panchayats.

The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) changed this by giving rural and urban local bodies a constitutional base. They came into force on 24 April 1993 (73rd, panchayats) and 1 June 1993 (74th, municipalities). About 2.5 lakh panchayats and several thousand urban bodies now work under them, with over 30 lakh elected representatives, of whom roughly 1.4 million are women.

Examiners ask: Why were these amendments needed? What are their main features? Have they made democracy real at the grassroots? The best answers compare ideals (Gandhi, Ambedkar, J.S. Mill, Tocqueville) with performance and name the weak spots: money, functions, officials, women's proxy rule.

Gandhi

In Hind Swaraj (1909) and later writings, he pictured India as a set of self-governing villages, "oceanic circles" in which each village is a republic and power flows from the bottom up.

B.R. Ambedkar

In the Constituent Assembly (4 November 1948) he asked what the village is but "a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism". He feared local elites and caste hierarchy. This is why the Constitution did not make panchayats a core feature.

J.S. Mill and Tocqueville

Mill (Considerations on Representative Government, 1861) saw local institutions as schools of citizenship. Tocqueville (Democracy in America, 1835) held that local liberties teach people how to use freedom.

Jayaprakash Narayan, Reconstruction of Indian Polity (1959)

Proposed a partyless, village-based pyramid of councils. Also Robert Putnam's Making Democracy Work (1993) links local associations to social capital and good government.

• Community Development Programme (1952) and National Extension Service (1953): top-down, officials led.
  • Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957): a three-tier system, with block as the key. Rajasthan launched it at Nagaur on 2 October 1959.
  • Ashok Mehta Committee (1977): two tiers, with the district as the main unit; political parties' role; reserved seats for SC/ST; a social audit.
  • G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985): bureaucratised planning ("grass without roots"); suggested the district as the unit.
  • L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986): recommended constitutional status and financial resources.
  • The 64th Amendment Bill (1989) passed the Lok Sabha but failed in the Rajya Sabha. The Narasimha Rao government passed the 73rd and 74th in 1992.

• Gram Sabha (Article 243A): all adult voters of the village. The base of the system.
  • Three tiers, except in states with a population below 20 lakh, which may skip the middle tier.
  • Direct elections to all seats; five-year term; fresh elections within six months if dissolved.
  • Reservation: seats for SC/ST in proportion to population; at least one-third for women (including within the SC/ST seats); states may reserve for OBCs. Many states raised women's reservation to 50%; Bihar did so first in 2006.
  • State Election Commission (Article 243K) runs the polls; State Finance Commission (243I) reviews finances every five years.
  • Eleventh Schedule: 29 subjects such as agriculture, health, education, drinking water, rural housing.
  • Exempt: Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, some hill areas of Manipur and Darjeeling (Article 243M).

• Three types (Article 243Q): Nagar Panchayat for a transitional area, Municipal Council for a smaller urban area and Municipal Corporation for a larger one.
  • Wards committees in cities with a population above three lakh.
  • Reservation for SC/ST and one-third for women; five-year term; State Election and Finance Commissions, as for panchayats.
  • Twelfth Schedule: 18 functions, including urban planning, regulation of land use, roads and bridges, water supply, public health, slum improvement and urban poverty alleviation.
  • District Planning Committee (Article 243ZD) to consolidate plans of panchayats and municipalities; Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE) for cities above a million.

Notice a key difference: the Twelfth Schedule functions are broader and more technical, but city mayors in many states are weak, elected indirectly or for one year, and parastatal agencies (development authorities, water boards) hold real power.

The 73rd Amendment did not apply to Fifth Schedule areas unless Parliament extended it. After the Bhuria Committee (1995), Parliament passed the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA).

  • The Gram Sabha is central: it approves plans and safeguards community resources, customs and culture.
  • Consultation before land acquisition and mining leases; ownership of minor forest produce; control over local markets and money-lending.
  • The Forest Rights Act, 2006 gave Gram Sabhas a role in recognising rights over forests. In Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment (the Niyamgiri case, 2013), the Supreme Court told Gram Sabhas of the Dongria Kondh to decide on the bauxite project, which rejected it.

PESA applies in ten states (Andhra, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan). Critics say that many states have not made rules in full and that PESA is weakly applied.

cards.h: Money: the weak link in local government
cards.b:
• State Finance Commissions (Articles 243I and 243Y) must recommend how state taxes are shared with local bodies, and what grants they get. Many states set them up late, and the reports are often not acted upon.
  • Central Finance Commission: since the 11th FC, it has recommended grants to supplement local bodies' funds based on the State Finance Commissions' reports. The 15th FC gave over four lakh crore rupees to rural and urban local bodies for 2021-26, partly tied to conditions like property-tax reform and accounts.
  • Own revenue: panchayats raise little, and urban bodies depend on property tax, which is under-collected. Octroi and entry taxes were removed with GST (2017), leaving cities with fewer independent sources.
  • Other tools: municipal bonds in a few cities, user charges, and central schemes channelled through local bodies.

Principle of subsidiarity: tasks should rest with the lowest level that can do them well. The Second ARC (2005-09) also urged that local bodies be given clear functions and the funds that go with them.

Achievements:

  • Regular elections; a large cohort of elected women (about 46% of panchayat members according to government data), SC/ST and OBC representatives.
  • Studies by Esther Duflo and Raghabendra Chattopadhyay (2004) found that women leaders invest more in public goods like drinking water.
  • Kerala's People's Plan Campaign (1996) transferred about 35-40% of the state's plan funds to local bodies.

Weaknesses:

  • The "3 Fs": functions, funds and functionaries are not devolved fully; the Eleventh Schedule is "may" not "shall". States hold the real power.
  • Low own revenue; dependence on grants (the 15th Finance Commission recommended over ₹4 lakh crore for local bodies in 2021-26).
  • Proxy rule by "sarpanch-pati" for women representatives.
  • Caste and elite capture; irregular Gram Sabhas.
  • Delayed urban elections; weak mayors.
  • Parallel bodies and schemes managed by departments.

• Supreme Court on OBC reservation: in Vikas Kishanrao Gawali (2021) the Court required a "triple test" (an empirical commission, proportion to data, and the 50% cap) before OBC quotas in local bodies.
  • Digital: eGramSwaraj portal, SVAMITVA property cards (2020), Gram Panchayat Development Plans and the annual People's Plan Campaign.
  • Proxy rule: a committee under the Ministry of Panchayati Raj studied the problem in 2023, and states are tightening rules.
  • Finance: grants to local bodies recommended by the 15th and 16th Finance Commissions.
  • Urban: Smart Cities Mission (2015) and AMRUT have been criticised for working through special-purpose bodies instead of municipalities.
  • J&K: after 2019, the 73rd and 74th Amendments apply; District Development Council elections were held in December 2020.

"Examine the 73rd and 74th Amendments. Have they strengthened grassroots democracy?"
"Why have panchayats failed to become institutions of self-government in practice?"
"Discuss the role of women in local government after reservation."
"Assess the PESA Act."

Structure: ideas (Gandhi, Ambedkar, Mill); committees from Balwant Rai Mehta to Singhvi; features of the 73rd and 74th Amendments with the Schedules; PESA and Forest Rights Act; achievements; the 3 Fs gap; proxy representation; reforms (devolution, own revenue, State Finance Commission follow-up, training); conclude that constitutional recognition is only the first step.
